V-Code Gem: 1970 Plymouth Superbird Is All-Original, Unrestored, and Numbers-Matching
11 photos
Photo: CARFINDER/YouTube
Unhappy with how the standard Charger and the improved Charger 500 fared on NASCAR ovals, Dodge created the radical Daytona in 1969 . Fitted with a long nose cone and a massive rear wing, it was unlike anything else available in dealerships. In 1970, Plymouth created its own version, the Superbird.
When the Daytona arrived, NASCAR homologation rules required that at least 500 units be produced for public consumption. Dodge built 503 examples, and they sold like hotcakes. In 1970, however, NASCAR raised the production requirement to one car for every two manufacturer's dealers in the United States. This rule forced Plymouth to build at least 1,920 Superbirds.
The company put together 1,935 units and struggled to sell them. Unsold Superbirds reportedly sat on dealer lots until as late as 1970, with some even converted to Road Runner specs simply because no one wanted them. As a result, the Superbird is more common than the Daytona on the classic car market. It's also more affordable when it comes to non-Hemi examples.
On the flip side, all-original, unrestored examples are hard to come by. And these cars tend to fetch big six-figure sums, usually changing hands for over a quarter-million bucks. The TorRed "winged warrior" you see here is one of those vehicles.
Speaking of powerplants, the Superbird was available with one of three V8 engines. Just like the Charger Daytona, it came standard with the four-barrel 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, with the mighty 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi on the options list. But it also got a mid-range option that the Daytona didn't have.
I'm talking about the six-barrel version of the 440 V8. The mill was introduced in 1969 on the Super Bee and Road Runner (part of the A12 package) and became widely available on B-body Mopars in 1970. The mill was rated at 390 horsepower, 15 more than the four-barrel 440.
Of the 1,935 Superbirds made, 135 were equipped with the Hemi, while 716 got the six-barrel option. The remaining units were fitted with the standard powerplant. This unrestored Superbird has the 6-BBL setup , confirmed by the V in its VIN. The mill is paired with a four-speed manual transmission, which narrows the production number to just 308 examples.
While survivor cars come with all sorts of flaws, this Superbird is an exception. I'm not saying it's flawless; I'm sure some issues may pop up at a closer look. But it's as close as it gets to being perfect, and that's mighty impressive for a Mopar that rolled off the assembly line a whopping 56 years ago as of 2026.
And that's precisely why it fetched big bucks at Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction, which is where it was sitting on display when the video below was recorded. The Superbird crossed the block for $368,500, a sum that also includes the buyer's premium.
This sticker places it among the five most expensive V-code Superbirds ever sold at public auction. It's also one of only four V-code examples that fetched over $350,000. The all-time record was set in 2023 by a numbers-matching, low-mileage survivor in Lemon Twist paint . It sold for $550,000.
That same year, a restored automatic Superbird fetched $401,500. Finally, the third most expensive V-code Superbird, a highly optioned example, traded for $375,000 in 2026. Hit the play button below to check out this gorgeous time capsule.
